\noindent{\small *Corresponding author: Jason Timm; jtimm@unm.edu}

# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Gutenberg Atlas is a book-level metadata dataset for English-language Project
Gutenberg. For 21,296 books, it provides publication years derived from
HathiTrust bibliographic matches, author lifespans, Wikidata gender and
citizenship claims, and stable identifiers linking the source records. Records
were linked deterministically to Wikidata authors and matched
to HathiTrust bibliographic holdings. In a stratified sample of 199 release
records, the derived years were within one year of sourced reference years for
87.4% (95% CI 82.7--92.1). The dataset supports historical corpus construction,
digital humanities, bibliographic research, and evaluation of metadata-linkage
methods.

**Keywords:** Project Gutenberg; HathiTrust; Wikidata; bibliographic metadata;
digital humanities; historical corpora

# Overview

Project Gutenberg is a large, continuously updated collection of
machine-readable books, but its catalog does not systematically record when a
work first appeared in print [@projectgutenberg_catalog]. Existing releases
provide only part of the metadata needed for historical research: PG-19
includes publication dates but targets language modeling [@rae2019compressive],
whereas the Standardized Project Gutenberg Corpus includes author lifespans
but not book-level first-publication years [@gerlach2020spgc]. Related work has
enriched German-language corpora with publication and demographic metadata
[@rohrbacher2025decorp; @rohrbacher2026bridging], while NovelTM documents
HathiTrust metadata for English-language fiction [@underwood2020noveltm].

Gutenberg Atlas combines book-level publication-year estimates, structured
author metadata, and sourced date validation for English Project Gutenberg in
one reproducible build. Wikidata work dates served only as a cross-check
because just 41 validation books matched a dated work. No book texts are
redistributed. The resource is intended for studies that need temporal and
author covariates on the same books without obscuring which archive supplied
each value.

## Repository location

**Repository:** <https://github.com/jaytimm/gutenberg-atlas>  
**Dataset DOI:** <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23628668>

The repository contains the frozen release, retained candidate
records with decision codes, validation records, documentation, build scripts, and
Supplementary File 1. The DOI identifies the archived version 1.0.0 release
[@timm2026atlas].

## Context

Project Gutenberg supplies catalog identity, HathiTrust bibliographic
evidence, and Wikidata structured author claims. Source fields are retained so
values remain traceable and reusable with Project Gutenberg texts. The release
also preserves excluded candidates and decision codes, allowing users to audit
coverage and apply different inclusion rules rather than treating the released
corpus as a neutral sample of publishing history.

# Method

## Steps

The build began with a frozen Project Gutenberg RDF catalog:
61,865 English-only text records [@projectgutenberg_catalog]. Restriction to
one named personal author and no other contributor left 38,550 eligible books,
excluding anonymous, multi-author, and most translated or edited works. The
monthly HathiTrust extract `hathi_full_20261001` was filtered to English books
[@hathitrust_hathifiles]. Normalized titles were matched within author surname,
first exactly and then by prefix containment. The earliest imprint in the best
tier became the year estimate. It is the earliest matched English-language
HathiTrust edition, not necessarily first publication; translations,
collections, and multi-volume sets require particular caution. For a
translation it may approximate the earliest matched English edition, while a
volume can inherit the date of a collected or multi-volume set.

Project Gutenberg agent identifiers were linked through Wikidata property
P1938, retaining human entities and their identifier, label, gender (P21),
citizenship (P27), birth (P569), and death (P570) claims. These are dated
source claims, not inferences from names or text [@vrandecic2014wikidata].
Project Gutenberg and Wikidata lifespans remain separate; conflicts are
flagged.

A released book required a HathiTrust match, a Wikidata human link, a year of
1700 or later, and an estimate between birth plus 15 and death plus five.
Project Gutenberg supplied lifespans, with Wikidata filling gaps and birth
plus 90 used when death was missing. Other eligible records remain in
`unverified_candidates.csv` with exclusion reasons.

Of 38,550 eligible books, 21,296 (55.2%) were released. Main exclusions were
no HathiTrust match (9,535), no Wikidata link (5,208), and an estimate more
than five years after death (2,251). Exclusion varied by author era
(Supplementary File 1).

## Sampling strategy

Publication-year accuracy was evaluated on 200 release books stratified by
five periods and two match tiers. At least eight books represented each cell;
remaining positions followed cell size. Sampling was without replacement
(seed 20261021); Supplementary File 1 gives the allocation.

## Quality control

Reference years were manually researched and stored with source URLs and
notes. Years were resolved for 199 books; one composite edition remained
unresolved. Accuracy meant agreement within one year. Cell estimates were
weighted to the release, with a stratified normal 95% confidence interval.
Sources included catalogues, digitized editions, reference works, and trade
listings. For 23 books the reference was a separate HathiTrust record and thus
not source-independent; excluding them gave 87.4% accuracy (95% CI
82.3--92.5). Other source restrictions changed accuracy by at most 1.2 points
(Supplementary File 1). Each reference note records what the cited year
represents, so users can distinguish evidence for first publication from dates
attached to particular editions. This distinction matters when dates anchor
narrow historical comparisons.

Weighted release accuracy was 87.4% (95% CI 82.7--92.1). Among 16 sampled
books dated 1925 or later, 10 were correct. This sparse stratum represents a
small share of the release and is reported as a limitation, not used as an
upper date boundary. Of 28 errors, 25 estimates were late (median +7 years),
usually reflecting a later edition or reprint.
Validation measured accuracy but did not alter release rows. Because screening
uses the estimated year, results apply only to released books, not the 17,254
excluded candidates; genuine posthumous editions may also be excluded.

```{r validation-by-period}
validation_table <- rbind(
  data.table(
    Period = "Release (weighted)",
    `Books judged` = date_summary[scope == "overall_weighted" & group == "all", judged],
    Accuracy = sprintf(
      "%.1f%% (95%% CI %.1f--%.1f)",
      date_summary[scope == "overall_weighted" & group == "all", accuracy_percent],
      date_summary[scope == "overall_weighted" & group == "all", ci_low_percent],
      date_summary[scope == "overall_weighted" & group == "all", ci_high_percent]
    )
  ),
  date_summary[scope == "period_unweighted", .(
    Period = group,
    `Books judged` = judged,
    Accuracy = sprintf("%.1f%%", accuracy_percent)
  )]
)
paper_table(
  validation_table,
  caption = "Publication-year accuracy in the release. The overall estimate is weighted; period rows are unweighted.",
  widths = c(2, 1.5, 2.8)
)
```

# Dataset Description

```{r release-at-a-glance}
n_eligible <- release_summary[metric == "eligible_books", value]
n_release <- nrow(release)
count_pct <- function(n, base, label) {
  sprintf("%s (%.1f%% of %s)", format(n, big.mark = ","), 100 * n / base, label)
}
at_a_glance <- data.table(
  Measure = c(
    "Eligible books", "Released books", "Distinct linked authors",
    "Publication years", "Gender coverage", "Citizenship coverage",
    "Flagged lifespan conflicts", "Flagged dates"
  ),
  Result = c(
    format(n_eligible, big.mark = ","),
    count_pct(n_release, n_eligible, "eligible"),
    format(uniqueN(release$agent), big.mark = ","),
    sprintf("%d--%d (median %d)", min(release$ht_year), max(release$ht_year),
            as.integer(median(release$ht_year))),
    count_pct(release[gender != "", .N], n_release, "released"),
    count_pct(release[country_of_citizenship != "", .N], n_release, "released"),
    count_pct(release[lifespan_conflict == TRUE, .N], n_release, "released"),
    count_pct(release[date_flag != "", .N], n_release, "released")
  )
)
paper_table(
  at_a_glance,
  caption = "Construction, coverage, and quality profile of Gutenberg Atlas.",
  widths = c(2.5, 3)
)
```

```{r year-figure, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=2.4, out.width="85%", fig.align="center", fig.pos="!htbp", fig.cap="Estimated publication years of the 21,296 released books, by decade."}
ggplot(release, aes(ht_year)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 10, boundary = 1700, fill = "grey35", color = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Estimated publication year", y = "Books") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Repository name:** Gutenberg Atlas (GitHub `jaytimm/gutenberg-atlas`, release v1.0.0)  
**Object names:** `release.csv`, `unverified_candidates.csv`, generated
summaries, validation files, build code, and documentation  
**Formats:** UTF-8 CSV (data); Markdown (documentation); R and Python
scripts (build code)  
**Creation dates:** 2026-10-20 to 2026-10-22  
**Dataset creator:** Jason Timm (conceptualization, methodology, software,
validation, curation, analysis, and documentation)  
**Language:** English variable names and documentation; books selected as
English in the Project Gutenberg catalog  
**License:** CC BY 4.0 (data); MIT (code)  
**Publication date:** 2026-10-24

The canonical `release.csv` has one row per Project Gutenberg identifier. It
records Gutenberg title and author fields; Wikidata identity, gender,
citizenship, and lifespan claims; mapped present-day citizenship; HathiTrust
year, item, imprint, match tier, and candidate count; and lifespan and date
flags. The data dictionary separates source claims, derived fields, and
validation results. Gender and citizenship retain Wikidata labels rather than
being inferred from names or texts. The present-day citizenship mapping is a
separate derived field, leaving users free to retain the historical claim or
apply a different geographic scheme.

Rows represent ebooks, not unique works. In total, 3,055 rows share a
HathiTrust item with another row (930 items). Work-level studies should
deduplicate on `htid` or title and author.

The date flag marks uncertain imprints, multi-volume or collected-works
titles, a single HathiTrust candidate, or more than 20 candidates; it describes
rather than excludes. Unweighted validation accuracy was 80% for flagged and
90% for unflagged books. These flags permit sensitivity analyses without
silently replacing or correcting the source-derived values.

`SOURCE_VERSIONS.md` documents snapshots and checksums;
`RELEASE_FREEZE.md` identifies published artifacts. HathiTrust permits
Hathifile reuse subject to contributing-institution restrictions
[@hathitrust_metadata_policy], and Wikidata is CC0. The 1.2 GB filtered
HathiTrust extract is not redistributed, but frozen match results permit
rebuilding the release without it.

# Reuse Potential

Gutenberg Atlas supplies temporal and author covariates for historical corpus
construction, stylometry, cultural analytics, book history, and teaching.
Project Gutenberg identifiers support text retrieval under title-level terms
and join directly to the Standardized Project Gutenberg Corpus
[@gerlach2020spgc].

## Worked reuse demonstration

As a reuse demonstration, models predicted broad genre, 25-year period, and
continuous year in five author-disjoint folds. Genre used 480 books; temporal
tasks used 1800--1924, an analytical window chosen for historical balance, not
a release boundary. Models received up to 5,000 body-text words. Penalized
models used word or character TF--IDF [@friedman2010glmnet]; a semantic model
averaged `BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5` chunk embeddings [@xiao2023bge].

```{r reuse-results}
model_names <- c(
  body_word = "Word TF-IDF", body_char = "Character TF-IDF",
  body_bge = "BGE embeddings"
)
task_names <- c(
  genre = "Broad genre", period = "Publication period",
  year = "Publication year"
)
best_body <- rbindlist(lapply(names(task_names), function(task_name) {
  candidates <- model_metrics[
    task == task_name & model %in% c("body_word", "body_char", "body_bge")
  ]
  if (task_name == "year") candidates[which.min(mae)] else candidates[which.max(macro_f1)]
}))
baseline <- model_metrics[model == "baseline"]
reuse_table <- merge(baseline, best_body, by = "task", suffixes = c("_baseline", "_body"))
sample_sizes <- model_sample[, .(Books = .N, Authors = uniqueN(agent)), by = task]
reuse_table <- merge(reuse_table, sample_sizes, by = "task")
reuse_table <- reuse_table[task %in% names(task_names)]
reuse_table[, task := factor(task, levels = names(task_names))]
setorder(reuse_table, task)
reuse_table[, `:=`(
  Task = unname(task_names[task]),
  Sample = sprintf("%s (%s)", Books, Authors),
  `Best body model` = unname(model_names[model_body]),
  Baseline = fifelse(
    task == "year", sprintf("%.1f years MAE", mae_baseline),
    sprintf("%.3f macro-F1", macro_f1_baseline)
  ),
  `Body-text result` = fifelse(
    task == "year", sprintf("%.1f years MAE", mae_body),
    sprintf("%.3f macro-F1", macro_f1_body)
  )
)]
paper_table(
  reuse_table[, .(Task, Sample, `Best body model`, Baseline, `Body-text result`)],
  caption = "Author-disjoint reuse demonstration. Sample gives books (authors). Lower mean absolute error (MAE) is better; higher macro-F1 is better.",
  widths = c(1.5, 1, 1.6, 1.5, 1.6)
)
```

Body text substantially improved genre prediction, whereas the best model
missed year by about 20 years on average. Raw file openings predicted time
better because front matter often prints dates; temporal-language studies
should therefore strip it. Supplementary File 1 gives full specifications,
controls, intervals, and confusion matrices. The exercise is not offered as a
benchmark leaderboard. It demonstrates two practical uses of the release:
constructing author-disjoint historical samples and testing whether apparent
temporal prediction comes from linguistic signal or printed metadata. Keeping
all books by an author in one fold also prevents the evaluation from rewarding
author recognition across train and test sets. The strong genre result shows
that the linked texts support controlled supervised tasks; the weaker temporal
result cautions that useful date covariates need not be readily recoverable
from body language alone.

## Limitations

Project Gutenberg reflects public-domain law, volunteer selection, and
preservation, not historical publishing. HathiTrust coverage is uneven and
earliest matches can be reprints, biasing estimated years and publication ages
later. Lifespan screening also truncates those errors. Wikidata claims are
incomplete, especially for citizenship, and were not independently
biographically validated. Provenance should be retained, and archive
composition should not be treated as evidence of historical authorship or
publication rates.
